title: A debugging mindset
body: Debug in a loop: reproduce, isolate, hypothesise, test, fix, prevent. Skipping a step (usually "reproduce") is how you end up changing code at random.
Reproduce first: find the smallest input and the exact steps that trigger the bug every time. A bug you can trigger on demand is half solved.
Isolate by halving the search space: comment out half the code path, feed simpler input, or check the value at the midpoint of the pipeline.
State one hypothesis you can test ("total is wrong because the loop skips the last item"), then run one experiment that proves or kills it.
Fix the cause, not the symptom. A null check that hides a NullPointerException is a symptom fix if the value should never have been null.
Prevent it coming back: turn your reproduction into a unit test that fails before the fix and passes after.
Change one thing at a time and keep notes. If you change three things and it works, you do not know which one fixed it.
example:
1. Reproduce: input "a,,b" -> crash, every time
2. Isolate:   split() OK, parse() crashes
3. Hypothesis: empty token "" reaches parseInt
4. Test:      print token before parseInt -> ""
5. Fix:       skip blank tokens
6. Prevent:   add test parse("a,,b")

title: Reading a stack trace
body: Line 1 gives the exception type and message. The type says what kind of failure; the message often names the bad value.
The frames below are the call stack, newest call first. The top frame is where the exception was thrown, which is often inside the JDK.
Scan down to the first frame in your own package. That is usually the line to inspect first, because your code passed the bad value in.
"Caused by:" introduces the exception that was wrapped. The root cause is usually the last "Caused by" block, so read it first.
"... 3 more" means the remaining frames are identical to the enclosing trace above it. Nothing is hidden that you cannot see elsewhere.
File name and line number (Config.java:34) let you jump straight there; most IDEs make them clickable in the console.
example:
Exception in thread "main"
  java.lang.IllegalStateException: bad config
  at app.Config.load(Config.java:21)
  at app.Main.main(Main.java:8)
Caused by: java.lang.NumberFormatException:
  For input string: "12a"
  at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(...)
  at app.Config.port(Config.java:34)   <- start
  at app.Config.load(Config.java:19)
  ... 1 more
(long lines wrapped to fit)

title: Compile errors, runtime exceptions, logic bugs
body: Compile errors stop javac before anything runs: "cannot find symbol", "incompatible types", "missing return statement". Fix the first error first; later ones are often knock-on effects.
Runtime exceptions happen while the program runs and come with a stack trace. The code is legal Java but hit a bad state, such as a null or an index out of range.
Logic bugs give no error at all: the program runs and prints the wrong answer. They are the hardest, because you must first know what the right answer is.
For logic bugs, write down the expected value at each step, then compare with the actual value using prints or a debugger until they diverge.
An off-by-one (< vs <=), integer division (5 / 2 == 2) and comparing strings with == are the classic logic bugs to check first.

title: Print debugging done well
body: Always label what you print: "total=" + total beats a bare 42 that you cannot match back to a variable.
Print before and after the suspect step so you see exactly where a value goes wrong.
Show boundaries and invisible characters by wrapping strings in brackets: "[" + s + "]" exposes leading spaces and empty strings.
Use Arrays.toString(arr) for arrays; printing an array directly gives something like [I@1b6d3586.
Print to System.err to keep debug output apart from real output, and delete the prints (or turn them into logging) once you are done.
If you are adding a fifth print and rerunning again, switch to a breakpoint: it shows every variable without editing code.

title: Breakpoints and the Variables view
body: A breakpoint pauses the program just before the marked line runs. Click the gutter next to a line number and start the program in debug mode, not normal run.
While paused, the Variables view shows every local variable, the parameters and the fields of this. Expand objects to drill into their fields.
The Frames (call stack) view lists how you got here. Click a lower frame to see that caller's variables at the moment of the call.
Put the breakpoint on the line before the crash or on the first line of the suspect method, not on the line after it.
A breakpoint that never hits tells you something too: that code path is not running at all.
Values shown are the state before the highlighted line executes. Step once to see the line's effect.
example:
Paused at Cart.java:14
Frames:            Variables:
> total()  :14       this = Cart@512
  checkout():31        items = ArrayList size=3
  main()   :8        i = 2
                     sum = 37.5

title: Step over, into, out and resume
body: Step over runs the current line, including any method calls on it, and stops on the next line of the same method.
Step into enters the method called on the current line. Use it when you suspect that method returns the wrong thing.
Step out finishes the current method and stops back in the caller, right after the call. Use it when you stepped into something uninteresting.
Resume (continue) runs until the next breakpoint is hit or the program ends.
Most IDEs skip JDK and library classes on step into by default; if you land in one anyway, step out.
"Run to cursor" runs to the line you clicked without adding a breakpoint, which saves stepping through a long loop.
example:
8  int n = parse(input);   // step INTO parse()
9  int r = square(n);      // step OVER square()
10 print(r);               // RESUME to next bp

inside parse():
21   String t = s.trim();
22   return Integer.parseInt(t); // step OUT

title: Watches and evaluate expression
body: A watch is an expression the debugger re-evaluates every time it pauses, such as items.size() or user.getName().
Watch derived values you would otherwise work out in your head: i < list.size(), total / count, s.length().
Evaluate expression runs any Java expression in the paused frame, such as map.get("key") or list.stream().filter(x -> x < 0).count().
Evaluating code with side effects (list.remove(0), iterator.next()) changes program state for real, so the rest of the run may behave differently.
Many IDEs let you set a variable's value while paused. That is a quick way to test "would it work if x were 0?" without a rebuild.
example:
Watches (paused at line 14):
  i                     = 3
  i < items.size()      = false   <- loop ends
  items.get(i - 1)      = "milk"
  total / items.size()  = 12

Evaluate: items.contains("eggs")  -> false

title: Beginner exceptions cheat sheet
body: NullPointerException: you called a method or read a field on null. Find which reference is null, then ask why it was never set.
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: an index is < 0 or >= length. Look for <= in a loop bound or length used where length - 1 was meant.
NumberFormatException: Integer.parseInt or similar got text that is not a number, such as "", " 42" or "4.5". Print the input in brackets.
ClassCastException: a cast to a type the object is not, often from raw collections or Object. The message names both classes.
ArithmeticException: "/ by zero" from integer division or modulo by 0. Double division gives Infinity or NaN instead of throwing.
IndexOutOfBoundsException (lists) and StringIndexOutOfBoundsException (substring, charAt) work like the array version.
example:
NullPointerException      -> what is null?
ArrayIndexOutOfBounds...  -> check loop bounds
NumberFormatException     -> print "[" + s + "]"
ClassCastException        -> what is the real type?
ArithmeticException       -> divisor is 0

java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException:
  Index 3 out of bounds for length 3

title: Conditional breakpoints and hit counts
body: A conditional breakpoint only pauses when a boolean expression is true, such as id == 4711 or name.equals("bob"). Ideal for the one bad item in 10,000.
Write null-safe conditions: "bob".equals(name) will not throw when name is null.
A hit count (pass count) pauses on the Nth hit. Use it when the bug shows up on, say, the 500th iteration.
Conditions are evaluated on every hit, which can slow a tight loop a lot. If it crawls, add a temporary if-block in code and break inside it.
A logging breakpoint (logpoint, or a breakpoint set not to suspend) prints an expression without pausing: print debugging without editing code.
Dependent breakpoints ("only enable after breakpoint X is hit") let you skip startup noise and stop only in the flow you care about.

title: Exception breakpoints
body: An exception breakpoint pauses at the moment an exception is thrown, with all local variables still intact, before any catch block runs.
Break on uncaught exceptions to stop where the crash starts rather than reading the stack trace after the fact.
Break on caught exceptions to find errors that are swallowed by catch (Exception e) {} or turned into a vague message further up.
Narrow it to one type (e.g. java.lang.NullPointerException) and, if your IDE supports it, a class filter like com.myapp.*. Otherwise JDK and framework internals trigger it constantly.
From the paused frame, walk the Frames view upward to see which of your calls passed in the bad value.

title: Reproduce with a failing unit test
body: Before fixing, write a test that fails because of the bug. It proves you have reproduced it and it guards against the bug returning.
Keep the test minimal: the smallest input that still triggers the failure. Shrinking the input often reveals the cause on its own.
Use assertEquals(expected, actual) in that order so the failure message reads correctly; use assertThrows for expected exceptions.
Debug the test itself: set a breakpoint in production code and run the single test in debug mode. That beats restarting the whole app.
Name the test after the behaviour ("parsesEmptyField"), not the ticket number, so it still makes sense later.

title: Logging instead of println
body: Use a logging API (SLF4J with Logback or Log4j 2, or java.util.logging) so you can switch detail on and off by configuration, without editing code.
SLF4J levels from noisy to severe: TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR. java.util.logging uses FINEST, FINER, FINE, CONFIG, INFO, WARNING, SEVERE.
Use {} placeholders: log.debug("id={}", id). The message is only formatted if DEBUG is enabled, so it is cheap when off.
Pass the exception as the last argument, log.error("load failed id={}", id, e), to get the full stack trace. Logging only e.getMessage() throws away the stack.
Turn on DEBUG for one package (e.g. com.myapp.billing) rather than everything, or the signal drowns.
Logger, timestamp and thread name in each line tell you who logged, when, and on which thread, which println never does.

title: Fail fast: requireNonNull and assertions
body: The earlier a bad value is rejected, the closer the stack trace is to the real mistake. A null stored now and used an hour later is very hard to trace.
Objects.requireNonNull(x, "x") in constructors and public methods throws immediately with a clear message.
Objects.checkIndex(i, size) (Java 9+) validates an index and throws IndexOutOfBoundsException with the values in the message.
assert cond : "message"; checks internal invariants, but assertions are off by default. Enable them with java -ea (Maven Surefire enables them for tests by default).
Never put required behaviour inside an assert: with assertions disabled the expression is not evaluated at all.
Throw IllegalArgumentException for bad arguments and IllegalStateException for calls made in the wrong state, and include the bad value in the message.

title: Helpful NullPointerException messages
body: Since Java 14 (on by default from Java 15, JEP 358) the NPE message says what was null and what was being done with it.
"Cannot invoke X because Y is null": Y is the null reference and X is the method you tried to call on it.
In a chain like a.getB().getC().name(), the message pins down which link returned null, so you do not need to split the line to find out.
Fields appear as "this.name" or "Main.cache", array elements as "arr[i]", and method results as the return value of a named method.
Local variables show as "<local4>" unless the class was compiled with debug info (javac -g). Maven and Gradle include it by default.
The message tells you where, not why. Next, find where that reference should have been set.
example:
String city = order.getCustomer()
                   .getAddress().city();

Exception in thread "main"
  java.lang.NullPointerException:
  Cannot invoke "Address.city()" because
  the return value of
  "Customer.getAddress()" is null

-> getCustomer() was fine; getAddress()
   returned null

title: Debugging collections: equals and hashCode
body: If set.contains(x) or map.get(key) unexpectedly misses, suspect equals/hashCode first: overriding equals without hashCode breaks HashSet and HashMap.
Check the contract in evaluate expression: a.equals(b) and a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() should both be true for keys you think are the same.
Mutating a field used in hashCode after inserting the object "loses" it: it now sits in the wrong bucket, and contains returns false.
System.identityHashCode(a) == System.identityHashCode(b) tells you whether two references are literally the same object.
equals(Object o) must take Object. Writing equals(Point p) creates an overload that collections never call.
Records, or IDE-generated equals/hashCode over the same fields, avoid most of these bugs. Use immutable keys.

title: Bisecting a regression with git bisect
body: When something worked in an older version and fails now, git bisect binary-searches the commits between to find the one that broke it.
Mark the current commit bad and a known working tag or commit good. Git checks out the midpoint; you test and mark it good or bad.
1,000 commits take only about 10 steps, because each step halves the range.
Automate it with git bisect run <cmd>: exit code 0 means good, 1-127 means bad, and 125 means "cannot test, skip this commit".
A focused failing test makes the perfect bisect command. Always finish with git bisect reset to return to your branch.
example:
git bisect start
git bisect bad                 # HEAD is broken
git bisect good v2.3.0         # this worked

# manual: build, test, then one of:
git bisect good    # or: git bisect bad

# or automatic:
git bisect run ./mvnw -q test \
    -Dtest=CsvParserTest#parsesEmptyField

# -> "abc123 is the first bad commit"
git bisect reset

title: Thread dumps and thread states
body: A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread's stack. Take one when an app hangs, is slow, or burns CPU: jstack <pid> or jcmd <pid> Thread.print.
Find the pid with jcmd (no arguments) or jps -l. Run the tools as the same OS user as the JVM.
RUNNABLE means running or ready to run. Threads blocked in native socket reads also show RUNNABLE, so check the top frame.
BLOCKED means waiting to enter a synchronized block held by another thread; look for "waiting to lock <0x...>" and find who holds it.
WAITING / TIMED_WAITING means parked in wait(), join(), sleep(), LockSupport.park or a queue take(). That is normal for idle pool threads.
Take 3 dumps 5-10 seconds apart. A thread stuck in the same frame in all three is your suspect; one that keeps moving is just busy.
example:
jcmd                       # list JVMs and pids
jcmd 4242 Thread.print > dump1.txt
jstack -l 4242 > dump2.txt # -l: lock details

"worker-3" #21 prio=5 ... waiting for monitor
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object
   monitor)
  at app.Cache.get(Cache.java:40)
  - waiting to lock <0x...a1> (a app.Cache)
  at app.Api.handle(Api.java:17)

title: Spotting deadlocks
body: A deadlock is two or more threads each holding a lock the other needs. CPU stays low and the affected requests never complete.
jstack and jcmd Thread.print detect monitor and ReentrantLock deadlocks automatically and print "Found one Java-level deadlock" at the end of the dump.
The report lists each thread, the lock it waits for, and which thread holds that lock: a cycle.
Programmatically, ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() returns the ids of deadlocked threads, which is useful in health checks.
The usual cause is acquiring two locks in different orders (A then B vs B then A). Fix it with a global lock order, or tryLock with a timeout.
Lots of BLOCKED threads without a cycle is lock contention, not a deadlock. Find the holder and see why it holds the lock so long.
example:
Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"t1":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x...
  (object 0x...b2, a app.Account),
  which is held by "t2"
"t2":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x...
  (object 0x...a1, a app.Account),
  which is held by "t1"

Fix: always lock the lower account id first

title: Debugging threads: suspend policies
body: A breakpoint can suspend all threads or only the thread that hit it. JDWP calls these SUSPEND_ALL and SUSPEND_EVENT_THREAD; IDEs show "All" vs "Thread" (or "Suspend VM" vs "Suspend thread").
Suspend all freezes the world, so state cannot change under you while you inspect it. But timeouts, heartbeats and other threads all stop too.
Suspend thread lets other threads keep running. Use it for servers and to catch two threads arriving at the same breakpoint.
Pausing changes timing, so races often vanish under the debugger (a "heisenbug"). Prefer logpoints (non-suspending breakpoints) or a thread dump for timing bugs.
In the Threads view you can switch between paused threads and inspect each one's stack, which is handy for confirming a lock-order problem.
Add the thread name to your conditions or logpoints (Thread.currentThread().getName()) to see who arrives when.
example:
Breakpoint at Inventory.java:52
  Suspend: Thread        (not All)
  Condition:
    Thread.currentThread().getName()
        .startsWith("http-nio")

Logpoint (no suspend):
  Thread.currentThread().getName()
    + " stock=" + stock

title: Heap dumps and Eclipse MAT
body: A heap dump is a snapshot of every object on the heap. Take one when memory keeps growing or after an OutOfMemoryError.

On demand: jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/app.hprof. Use an absolute path, since a relative one resolves against the target JVM's working directory. By default only live objects are dumped, after a full GC.
Automatically: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps. Set this in production so the evidence exists when the OOM happens.
In Eclipse MAT, start with the Leak Suspects report, then the dominator tree sorted by retained heap.
Shallow size is the object itself; retained size is everything that would be freed if it went away. A small HashMap retaining 2 GB is the leak.
Use "Path to GC Roots" (excluding weak/soft references) to see why a suspect object is still reachable, e.g. a static cache or a listener list.
Dumps are roughly heap-sized, pause the JVM while being written, and contain sensitive data. Treat them like a database backup.
example:
jcmd 4242 GC.heap_dump /tmp/app.hprof

java -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
     -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps -jar app.jar

MAT dominator tree:
Class                   Shallow  Retained
app.SessionCache          24 B    1.9 GB
 java.util.HashMap        48 B    1.9 GB
  java.util.HashMap$Node[] ...    1.9 GB

title: Class histograms: a cheap memory look
body: A class histogram lists instance counts and bytes per class. It is much faster and smaller than a full heap dump.
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram or jmap -histo:live <pid>. Both live variants force a full GC first, which pauses the app.
jmap -histo <pid> (no :live) skips the GC and includes garbage, which is cheaper but noisier.
Take two histograms minutes apart and diff them. Classes whose counts only ever grow are your leak candidates.
[B (byte[]), [C, java.lang.String and HashMap$Node usually top the list. Look for your own classes ranked unexpectedly high.
A histogram tells you what is piling up, not who holds it. Follow up with a heap dump and Path to GC Roots.
example:
jcmd 4242 GC.class_histogram | head -8

 num  #instances    #bytes  class name
---------------------------------------
   1:   1203345  96267600  [B
   2:   1201877  28845048  java.lang.String
   3:    600112  19203584  app.AuditEvent
   4:    600112  14402688  java.util.HashMap$Node
...
# AuditEvent count grows every minute

title: Reading GC logs
body: Enable unified GC logging (JDK 9+) with -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags. Add filecount=5,filesize=20m to rotate.
Each pause line shows the GC type, heap before->after(total) and pause time. Watch the "after" number over time.
If heap-after-GC keeps rising across many collections, live data is growing: a leak or an unbounded cache.
Frequent young pauses with flat heap-after mean high allocation rate. Profile allocations rather than adding heap.
Repeated "Pause Full" collections that recover little memory mean the heap is nearly full of live data; an OutOfMemoryError is near.
Logging is cheap enough for production. Turn it on before an incident, not after.
example:
java -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags\
:filecount=5,filesize=20m -jar app.jar

[12.3s][info][gc] GC(41) Pause Young (Normal)
  (G1 Evacuation Pause) 812M->301M(1024M) 9.8ms
[95.1s][info][gc] GC(97) Pause Young (Normal)
  (G1 Evacuation Pause) 900M->702M(1024M) 14ms
[96.0s][info][gc] GC(98) Pause Full
  (G1 Compaction Pause) 1020M->998M(1024M) 2.1s
-> live set ~1 GB in a 1 GB heap
(long lines wrapped to fit)

title: Java Flight Recorder and Mission Control
body: JFR is a low-overhead event recorder built into the JDK (free in OpenJDK 11+). It records CPU samples, allocations, locks, GC, I/O and exceptions.
Start at launch: -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=120s,filename=rec.jfr. The default settings target about 1% overhead; settings=profile records more detail.
Attach to a running JVM: jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=r settings=profile, then jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=r filename=/tmp/rec.jfr, then JFR.stop name=r.
Open the .jfr in JDK Mission Control (JMC, a separate download). Method Profiling shows hot methods; Lock Instances shows contention; Allocations shows who creates garbage.
No GUI? jfr summary rec.jfr gives event counts, and jfr print --events jdk.ExecutionSample rec.jfr dumps raw samples.
Keep a continuous recording in production (maxage=1h, disk=true) so you can dump the last hour right after an incident.
example:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=120s,\
filename=rec.jfr -jar app.jar

jcmd 4242 JFR.start name=r settings=profile
jcmd 4242 JFR.dump name=r filename=/tmp/rec.jfr
jcmd 4242 JFR.stop name=r

jfr summary /tmp/rec.jfr
jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter \
    /tmp/rec.jfr | head -40

title: Remote debugging with JDWP
body: Start the JVM with the JDWP agent and attach your IDE's "Remote JVM Debug" configuration to the port: same breakpoints and stepping as locally.
suspend=n starts the app normally; suspend=y waits for a debugger before main runs, which is useful for startup bugs.
Since JDK 9, address=5005 listens on localhost only; address=*:5005 listens on all interfaces. Anyone who reaches that port can run arbitrary code in your JVM.
Prefer keeping it on localhost and tunnelling: ssh -L 5005:localhost:5005 host, or kubectl port-forward pod/app 5005:5005.
The source you have open must match the deployed build, or line numbers and breakpoints will be off.
A suspend-all breakpoint in a shared environment freezes everyone's requests. Use thread-only suspension or logpoints there.
example:
java -agentlib:jdwp=transport=dt_socket,\
server=y,suspend=n,address=*:5005 -jar app.jar

# safer: bind locally, tunnel in
java -agentlib:jdwp=transport=dt_socket,\
server=y,suspend=n,address=5005 -jar app.jar
ssh -L 5005:localhost:5005 user@host

# command-line debugger
jdb -connect com.sun.jdi.SocketAttach:\
hostname=localhost,port=5005

title: Reading bytecode with javap
body: javap -c -p Foo.class disassembles every method, private ones included. Add -v for the constant pool, line tables and flags.
Use it when the source "obviously" cannot behave as it does: hidden autoboxing, string concatenation, synthetic bridge methods or lambdas.
Integer.valueOf / intValue calls reveal boxing, the usual source of surprise NPEs and == comparisons that fail above 127.
Since Java 9, string + compiles to invokedynamic makeConcatWithConstants; lambdas become invokedynamic plus a private lambda$name$0 method.
Check that the class you are running is the one you think: javap -v shows the class file version (major 61 = Java 17), and a stale class shows the old logic.
The LineNumberTable from javap -l maps bytecode offsets to source lines, which helps explain odd stepping in the debugger.
example:
// Integer count = map.get(k); int n = count;
javap -c -p Main.class

  10: invokeinterface #4  // Map.get
  15: checkcast     #5    // class Integer
  18: astore_2
  19: aload_2
  20: invokevirtual #6    // Integer.intValue
  23: istore_3            // NPE here if null

javap -v Main.class | grep major
  major version: 61

title: Class loading and initialisation failures
body: ClassNotFoundException (checked) comes from loading a class by name (Class.forName, loadClass) when it is not on the classpath, typically a missing driver or plugin jar.
NoClassDefFoundError means the class was there at compile time but cannot be loaded now: a missing jar at runtime, or a class whose static initialiser failed earlier.

ExceptionInInitializerError wraps an exception thrown in a static initialiser. Every later use of that class throws "NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class X", so look for the first error in the log.
NoSuchMethodError and NoSuchFieldError usually mean two versions of a library: you compiled against one and run with another. Check mvn dependency:tree or gradle dependencies.
Find out which jar a class actually came from with -verbose:class or -Xlog:class+load=info; each line shows the source location.
At runtime, Foo.class.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource() in evaluate expression also reveals the jar.
example:
java -Xlog:class+load=info -jar app.jar \
  | grep JsonParser
[0.412s][info][class,load] com.x.JsonParser
  source: file:/app/lib/json-1.2.jar   <- old!

Exception in thread "main"
  java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError:
  Could not initialize class app.Config
-> scroll up for the first error:
  java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError
  Caused by: java.lang.NumberFormatException

title: Profiling CPU and allocations
body: Do not guess where time goes: measure. Profile under realistic load, since a cold JVM spends its time in the interpreter and JIT.
async-profiler is a widely used open-source sampling profiler for Linux and macOS. It avoids safepoint bias and sees native and kernel frames.
Read a flame graph bottom-up: width is the share of samples, height is stack depth. Look for wide plateaus near the top; colours carry no meaning for cost.
Profile more than CPU: -e alloc finds allocation hotspots that drive GC, -e lock finds contention, and -e wall includes threads that are waiting (I/O, locks).
JFR with settings=profile gives method sampling with no extra install; open it in JMC or convert it to a flame graph.
For better accuracy with JFR and other JVM-based profilers, add -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+DebugNonSafepoints.
example:
# async-profiler 3.x (older: profiler.sh)
asprof -d 30 -e cpu -f /tmp/cpu.html 4242
asprof -d 30 -e alloc -f /tmp/alloc.html 4242
asprof -d 30 -e wall -t -f /tmp/wall.html 4242

# JDK only
jcmd 4242 JFR.start settings=profile \
     duration=30s filename=/tmp/cpu.jfr

title: JMH, JIT and why microbenchmarks lie
body: A hand-written timing loop measures the interpreter, then the JIT compiling, then dead code elimination, not your code. Use JMH for microbenchmarks.
Dead code: if a result is never used, the JIT may delete the work. Return it from the @Benchmark method or pass it to Blackhole.consume.
Constant folding: inputs known at compile time get precomputed. Keep inputs in @State fields, not literals or static finals.
Run warm-up iterations and several forks (@Fork); JIT decisions differ between runs. Read the error margin, not just the mean.
Use -XX:+PrintCompilation or -Xlog:jit+compilation=debug to see methods being compiled or deoptimised ("made not entrant") mid-run.
Safepoint bias: many profilers only sample at safepoints, so cost gets blamed on the wrong line. Confirm hot spots with two tools.
A microbenchmark win may not matter in the real app. Confirm with a production-like load test and a profile.

title: Debugging in containers and production
body: JDK 17 is container-aware: heap defaults come from the container memory limit. Size it with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 rather than a fixed -Xmx that ignores the limit.
Run JDK tools inside the container as the same user as the JVM: kubectl exec -it pod -- jcmd 1 Thread.print. Distroless or JRE-only images may not include jcmd, so plan for it.

-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError makes the JVM exit on OOM so the orchestrator restarts it, instead of limping on half-broken. Pair it with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError and a mounted volume as HeapDumpPath.
Log structured JSON with a correlation ID on every line (SLF4J MDC) so you can follow one request across threads and services.
Check the JVM's effective settings with jcmd 1 VM.flags and jcmd 1 VM.system_properties; startup scripts often override what you think you set.
Prefer read-only evidence in production (thread dumps, JFR, logs, metrics) over attaching a debugger.

title: Flaky tests and nondeterminism
body: A test that sometimes fails has a hidden input: time, randomness, thread scheduling, iteration order of HashMap/HashSet, test order, or the network.
Make randomness reproducible: create new Random(seed), log the seed on failure, and replay that seed locally.
Inject a java.time.Clock instead of calling Instant.now() so tests can use Clock.fixed(...). Watch for time-zone and DST assumptions.
Run the test many times to make it fail on demand: @RepeatedTest(500), or loop it in CI. Check for order dependence with @TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.Random.class).
Replace Thread.sleep waits with explicit synchronisation (CountDownLatch, or Awaitility's await().until(...)).
For memory-model and race bugs, use jcstress (OpenJDK Code Tools): it runs actor methods concurrently millions of times and counts each observed outcome.

title: Off-heap and native memory
body: Process RSS can exceed -Xmx by a lot: metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, GC structures, direct ByteBuffers and native libraries all live outside the heap.
Enable Native Memory Tracking with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary (it must be set at startup and costs some performance), then run jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.
To find growth: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline, wait, then jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff.
NMT only tracks memory the JVM itself allocates. Memory malloc'ed by native libraries (JNI, some compression or crypto libs) does not appear there; compare NMT's total with RSS from ps or pmap.
Thread count times stack size (-Xss, often 1 MB) adds up. A thread leak shows as a growing "Thread" section and eventually "unable to create native thread".
Cap direct buffers with -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize and metaspace with -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize so leaks fail loudly instead of the OS killing the process.
example:
java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -jar app.jar

jcmd 4242 VM.native_memory baseline
# ...wait while it grows...
jcmd 4242 VM.native_memory summary.diff

Total: reserved=3.1GB +410MB, committed=1.9GB +405MB
- Java Heap  committed=1024MB +0MB
- Thread     committed=402MB +380MB
             (threads #398 +370)   <- leak
- Metaspace  committed=98MB +2MB

title: Post-mortem: OOM killer, Java OOM and crashes
body: Java OutOfMemoryError: the JVM throws it with a reason. "Java heap space" (live data too big or a leak), "Metaspace" (class leak), "Direct buffer memory", "unable to create native thread".
Linux OOM killer: the process just vanishes with no Java stack trace and no hs_err file, exit code 137 (SIGKILL). Check dmesg, or "OOMKilled" in kubectl describe pod.
An OOM kill means total RSS exceeded the container or host limit, usually heap plus native memory. Lower MaxRAMPercentage or find the native growth with NMT.
A hard JVM crash (SIGSEGV etc.) writes hs_err_pid<pid>.log to the working directory; set -XX:ErrorFile=/logs/hs_err_pid%p.log to choose where.
In hs_err, read the "Problematic frame" line: C = native code (often a JNI library), V = the JVM itself, J = JIT-compiled Java. Then read the thread stack and the loaded libraries.
Crashes in V or J frames are JVM bugs: upgrade to the latest patch release and search the JDK bug tracker for the frame name.
example:
$ dmesg | grep -i "killed process"
Out of memory: Killed process 4242 (java)
  total-vm:6.1GB, anon-rss:3.9GB ...

# hs_err_pid4242.log
# A fatal error has been detected by the
# Java Runtime Environment:
#  SIGSEGV (0xb) at pc=0x00007f..., pid=4242
# Problematic frame:
# C  [libzstd-jni.so+0x2a1f0]
-> native library bug, not your Java code
